name: Retinol peel (Retinoic acid peel)

lead: A retinoic acid peel applies a tretinoin solution in a clinic to treat photoaging, wrinkles, scars and pigment such as melasma. People use it for smoother, more even skin.

Tretinoin is a retinoid used topically for acne, melasma, scars and aging. As a peel it is applied in a higher concentration, often 5% in studies, to exfoliate the skin and stimulate renewal. Research includes a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in facial photoaging and comparative trials in acanthosis nigricans. A review notes the field lacks a consensus protocol.

paras: A clinician applies it, and it is later washed off or left to act depending on the protocol. It is often preceded by a Jessner's peel and done as a short series. Peeling and flaking follow for several days.
Reported risks include stinging, redness, dryness and pigment changes, rising with depth. Retinoids are generally avoided in pregnancy, and sun protection is important afterward.

angle.text: People use retinoic acid peels to smooth photoaged skin, soften scars and wrinkles, and fade pigment. The retinoid renews skin and stimulates collagen. Trials have studied it in facial photoaging and acanthosis nigricans.

lead: A retinoic acid (tretinoin) peel is a superficial chemical peel in which a retinoid solution, often at 5% concentration in studies, is applied to the skin in a clinic and later washed off or left to act [1][2]. A review describes it as a superficial peeling frequently performed in dermatological clinics in Brazil, with a first study on melasma published in 2001 [1]. Wikipedia describes retinoic acid peels as deeper than alpha-hydroxy acid peels, used for scars, wrinkles and pigment, and often preceded by a Jessner's peel [3].

Retinol peels (commonly 3 to 4 percent retinol in studies) and tretinoin peels (often 5 percent) are used to improve photoaging, melasma and skin texture, and have been compared with glycolic acid peels and with lasers in small trials [4][1][2][5][6]. A critical review states that studies have reported applicability with reasonable methodology but without a consistent scientific background or consensus [1].
infobox: Superficial; Wikipedia says deeper than BHA peels [3]

paras: Reported uses include melasma, skin aging, acne, scars and photodamage, as topical tretinoin is used for various dermatoses [1]. Wikipedia lists scars, wrinkles and pigment [3].

Dermatology reviews group the indications for topical tretinoin as acne, melasma, scars, skin aging and non-melanoma skin cancer; retinoid cellular receptors were reported in 1987, though the review notes that a direct cause-effect relation has not been established [1]. As a peeling agent, most reviewed studies reported benefits in melasma and skin aging, and the reviewers call for better-designed studies on concentration, vehicle and treatment interval [1]. Retinol-based peels are marketed as physician-strength products, with homecare regimens recommended alongside in the studies of them [5].

Wikipedia describes the retinoic acid peel as deeper than beta-hydroxy acid peels, used for scars, wrinkles and pigment, and usually preceded by a Jessner's peel, applied right beforehand so that the retinoic acid can penetrate; peeling occurs around the third day, and dramatic changes need multiple peels over time [3]. Light peels usually need no anesthesia [3].

Retinol peels use a different retinoid form. An advanced 3 percent retinol peel studied in 2019 contained retinol with other firming and volumizing ingredients, administered under physician direction at 6-week intervals, with a supportive homecare regimen; a related formula used in a case series contained 3 percent retinol, 4 percent triethyl citrate, 0.1 percent aminophil, bisabolol and 1 percent vitamin E acetate [5][7].

Photoaging: in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 45 patients aged 35 to 70 with moderate-to-severe photodamage, participants received three sessions of full-face microdermabrasion followed by either a 5% retinoic acid peel or placebo, to evaluate efficacy and tolerability [2].

Retinol peels: a 2019 clinical study of a 3% retinol peel with supportive homecare enrolled 24 women aged 18 to 65 with photodamage, acne, hyperpigmentation or melasma, including skin of color (Fitzpatrick types IV to VI). They received 2 to 4 peels at 6-week intervals (78 peels in total: photodamage group n=14 with an acne subgroup n=5; melasma n=5; skin of color n=5), with dermatologist grading, self-assessment and photography to document tolerability and efficacy [5]. A 2024 case series of four breast cancer patients treated with a 3% retinol peel at least 6 weeks after stopping post-surgical therapy reported improved skin brightness and firmness from 4 weeks onward and patient satisfaction [7]. A 2015 study measured the effect of a retinol peel on facial and neck skin lipids in women aged 50 to 69, measuring sebum with a Sebumeter before each of three peels [8].

Melasma: a randomized controlled study of 60 adults aged 18 to 60 compared a 35% glycolic acid peel with a 4% retinol peel, six sessions at two-week intervals, using modified MASI, dermoscopic scores and a melasma quality-of-life index. Both groups improved significantly (p<0.001) with no significant difference between them; mild, self-limiting adverse effects were more common in the retinol group (13.3 percent) than the glycolic acid group (3.3 percent) [6]. The original Brazilian retinoic acid study for melasma was published in 2001 [1].

Acanthosis nigricans: a split-neck comparison of 20 Egyptian patients had fractional CO2 laser on the right neck and a 5% retinoic acid peel on the left, four sessions two weeks apart, with a significant improvement in both groups on the ANASI score and in dermatologist and dermoscopic assessments [4]. A 2025 randomized trial compared the same two treatments [9], and a 2024 systematic review of six trials with 133 patients compared lasers with topical treatments including glycolic acid, retinoic acid and TCA peels and tretinoin cream [10].
A Brazilian review of tretinoin peels concluded the literature lacks consensus and called for controlled, randomized studies comparing tretinoin cream with its use as a peel [1].

Wikipedia notes that complications rise with peel depth and can include prolonged redness, pigment changes, milia and skin thinning, and that light peels commonly cause stinging, redness, irritation and dryness. [3]

In the melasma trial comparing peels, adverse effects were mild and self-limiting, reported in 13.3 percent of retinol-peel participants [6]. Wikipedia lists photosensitivity as a complication of chemical peels in general, and expects redness, with a yellowish tinge lasting a few hours in some people; both professional peels and low-concentration at-home kits carry risks of injury and scarring [3].

Chemical peeling was introduced in the second half of the 19th century by the Austrian dermatologist Ferdinand Ritter von Hebra, who used agents such as phenol, croton oil and nitric acid; the phenol-croton oil peel reached mainstream practice in the 1960s [3]. The tretinoin peel as a modern superficial technique was first reported by Cuce and colleagues in 2001 for melasma, and has been practiced often in Brazilian dermatology clinics [1].

timeline.event: Ferdinand Ritter von Hebra introduces chemical peeling with phenol, croton oil and nitric acid.[3]
First published study of the tretinoin peel, for melasma, by Cuce et al. [1].
Clinical study of a 3% retinol peel across photodamage, acne, melasma and skin of color.[5]
Randomized comparison of 35% glycolic acid and 4% retinol peels in melasma published.[6]
